tool.name: webpack
tool.tagline: Highly configurable bundler that turns your code, styles and images into optimized files
tool.description: webpack is the bundler that powered a decade of web development: starting from your app's main file it follows every import, converts CSS, images and other files with loaders and plugins, and writes a few optimized files for the browser. A huge number of live apps still build with it, and its ideas (loaders, code splitting, Module Federation) live on in newer tools such as Rspack.

glossary.def: A bundler: it follows every import from your app's starting file and combines your code, styles and images into a few files a browser can load.
In webpack, a small converter that takes one file, such as CSS or TypeScript, and turns it into a module webpack can bundle.
One finished output file written by a bundler, holding many of your modules combined.
A group of modules that a bundler writes out together as one file. Splitting an app into chunks lets code that isn't needed yet be downloaded later.
A small piece of code webpack adds to its output that, in the browser, runs your modules in the right order and downloads extra chunks when needed.
A short code computed from a file's contents and put in its name, like app.3f1c2a9b.js. It changes only when the contents change.
A much faster rewrite of webpack in Rust that accepts most webpack settings, loaders and plugins, so existing projects can switch with little work.
A programming language that turns into fast machine instructions and avoids many memory bugs. Many new JavaScript tools are written in it for speed.
A tool that rewrites newer JavaScript, and extras such as JSX, into older JavaScript that more browsers understand.
HTML-like tags written inside JavaScript, as React uses: <Button label="Hi" />. It must be converted to plain JavaScript before a browser can run it.
A popular extended version of CSS, with extras such as variables and nesting. It has to be converted to plain CSS before browsers can use it.
A CSS file (usually named *.module.css) whose class names are made unique to that file when imported, so two files can use the same class name without clashing.
webpack 5's built-in handling of images, fonts and other files: depending on the rule's type, importing one gives a URL, a data URI or the file's text.
A URL that holds the file itself, starting with data:, instead of pointing to where the file is. It saves a download for very small files.
A module that says it can take a new version of itself while the page runs. When a file changes, the nearest one is updated instead of reloading the page.
A file that links bundled, minified code back to your original files and lines, so error messages and browser developer tools show your real code.
Extra code that recreates a missing built-in feature, for example a newer browser function in old browsers, or a Node module in the browser.
An import of a package by its name, like import x from "react", instead of by a file path like "./x.js".
The part of a bundler that works out which file an import refers to: one in your project, or a package in node_modules.
Cutting an app's bundle into several files, so the browser downloads some code only when it's needed.
A special comment inside import(), such as /* webpackChunkName: "chart" */, that webpack reads to name a chunk or decide when to download it.
A rule in webpack's SplitChunksPlugin that collects matching modules, such as everything from node_modules, into a shared chunk.
Leaving code that nothing uses out of the bundle, like shaking a tree so the dead leaves fall.
The tool webpack uses by default to minify JavaScript in production builds.
Joining many modules into one shared scope instead of wrapping each in its own function, which makes the bundle smaller and faster.
A webpack feature that lets one separately built and deployed app load modules from another while the page runs, sharing packages such as React between them.
One part of a large website that its own team builds and deploys separately; the parts are put together in the browser.
In Module Federation, the app that loads modules from other, separately deployed builds (its remotes) while it runs.
In Module Federation, a separately deployed build that offers (exposes) some of its modules for host apps to load while they run.
The small library webpack is built on for its hooks: named moments in a build that plugins can attach functions to.
In webpack, a named moment in the build, such as 'compilation started' or 'files about to be written', that a plugin can attach a function to.
In webpack, the main object that runs a build from start to finish. Plugins receive it in apply(compiler) and attach functions to its hooks.
In webpack, one build of the dependency graph and its output files. In watch mode a new one is made for every rebuild.
The map of every module in a build and which module imports which, starting from the entry points.
webpack's map of which modules go into which chunks, and which chunks load which others.

concepts.name: What webpack does
concepts.summary: webpack starts from your main file, follows every import to map out your whole app, and writes a few combined files the browser can load.
concepts.why: Many live apps still build with webpack, and its ideas explain how every bundler works.
concepts.body:
In the modules lesson you split code into files that `import` each other, and met the **bundler**: a tool that combines those files for the browser. A real website may have hundreds of your own modules, plus npm packages, CSS and images. Loading each one separately would be slow, and browsers can't load some of them at all. **webpack** is the bundler that powered most big websites for a decade, and many still use it.

webpack works in steps. It starts from an **entry point**, the file where your app starts (by default `./src/index.js`). It reads that file, follows every `import` (and `require()`), then follows the imports of those files, and so on. The result is the **dependency graph**: a map of every file your app needs and which file uses which.

Files that aren't plain JavaScript, such as CSS, TypeScript or images, go through **loaders**: small converters that turn each file into something webpack understands. That way CSS, images and fonts become part of the graph too.

webpack then groups the modules into **chunks** and writes each chunk out as a **bundle**: one finished file the browser downloads. Alongside goes a tiny piece of code, the **webpack runtime**, that lets the modules find each other in the browser.

Everything else is done by **plugins**: add-ons that step in at any point of the build. Plugins create the HTML page, put CSS in its own file, insert settings and **minify** the code (remove spaces, comments and long names so it downloads faster but works the same).

Remember four words: **entry** (where to start), **output** (where to write bundles), **loaders** and **plugins**. Add **mode**, which picks sensible settings for development or for production.

webpack is extremely flexible. That is its strength and its cost: settings can grow long, and builds are slower than with newer tools. New projects usually start with Vite, a newer and faster tool of the same kind, or with the tools that come with React and similar libraries. Existing webpack apps often move to **Rspack**, a much faster rewrite that accepts most of the same settings. What you learn here carries over to both.
concepts.code:
# Smallest setup: no config file needed for the defaults
mkdir wp-demo && cd wp-demo && npm init -y
npm install -D webpack webpack-cli
mkdir src
echo 'import { greet } from "./greet.js"; console.log(greet("Ann"));' > src/index.js
echo 'export const greet = (n) => `Hello, ${n}`;' > src/greet.js

npx webpack --mode production       # reads src/index.js, writes dist/main.js
# asset main.js 49 bytes [emitted] [minimized] (name: main)
# ./src/index.js + 1 modules ...
# webpack compiled successfully

node dist/main.js      # Hello, Ann
takeaways: Entry -> dependency graph -> chunks -> bundles
Loaders convert files; plugins step in anywhere in the build
Defaults: entry ./src/index.js, output dist/main.js
Rspack is a faster tool that accepts most webpack settings
pitfalls: Hand-writing a webpack setup for a brand-new project when Vite or a ready-made starter would do.

quiz.q: What does webpack build before writing any bundle?
options: A zip file of your project
A dependency graph, starting from the entry points
A list of your npm scripts
quiz.explain: webpack follows imports from the entries to find every module that belongs in the output.

concepts.name: Configuration: entry, output and mode
concepts.summary: Write webpack.config.js with entry, output and mode, put content hashes in file names, and empty the output folder on each build.
concepts.why: Every webpack project starts from this skeleton.
concepts.body:
Without settings, webpack reads `src/index.js` and writes `dist/main.js`. To change anything, create `webpack.config.js` in the project folder. It's an ordinary Node file that exports a settings object (or a function that returns one), usually with `module.exports`, Node's older CommonJS style.

The essentials:

- `entry`: the start file. Give an object to make several separate bundles: `{ app: "./src/app.js", admin: "./src/admin.js" }`.
- `output.path`: the output folder, as an absolute path. `path.resolve(__dirname, "dist")` builds one; `__dirname` is the folder this settings file is in.
- `output.filename`: the bundle's file name, with placeholders in square brackets that webpack fills in: `[name]` (the entry's name) and `[contenthash]`, as in `[name].[contenthash].js`.
- `output.clean: true`: empty the output folder before each build.
- `output.publicPath`: the start of the URL the files will be served from, such as `"/"`.

A **content hash** is a short code computed from a file's contents, like `3f1c2a9b`. It changes only when the contents change. Putting it in file names lets browsers keep files for a long time, because a changed file always arrives under a new name.

`mode` picks a set of defaults:

- `"development"`: readable output, fast rebuilds, helpful error messages.
- `"production"`: minified output with unused code left out, and `process.env.NODE_ENV` set to `"production"`.

Without a mode, webpack warns and assumes production.

Run webpack with `npx webpack` (reads `webpack.config.js`), `npx webpack --config other.config.js` or `npx webpack --mode development`, and put those commands in npm scripts.

Exporting a **function** `(env, argv) => config` lets one file serve several modes: `argv.mode` holds the mode you typed in the terminal, and `--env foo=bar` arrives as `env.foo`.
takeaways: `entry` names the bundles; `output.path` must be an absolute path
`[name]` and `[contenthash]` placeholders fill in file names
`mode` switches on development or production defaults
Export a function to vary settings by mode and --env
pitfalls: Leaving out `mode`: you get a warning and slower production-style builds while developing.

quiz.q: Why use `[contenthash]` in production file names?
options: Names change only when contents change, so browsers can keep files for a long time
quiz.explain: Browsers can keep hashed files for a long time, because new content always gets a new name.

concepts.name: Loaders
concepts.summary: Convert files with module.rules (test, use, exclude), chain loaders right to left, and handle CSS and newer JavaScript.
concepts.why: Loaders are how webpack handles anything beyond plain JavaScript.
concepts.body:
Out of the box, webpack understands JavaScript and JSON. Loaders teach it other kinds of files, or change code on the way in. You list them under `module.rules`; each rule says which files it is for and which loaders to use:

- `test`: which files, usually written as a **regular expression**: a pattern for matching text, between slashes. `/\.css$/i` means "ends in .css", ignoring capitals (that's the `i`).
- `use`: one loader, or a list of loaders (each can have an `options` object).
- `exclude` / `include`: skip or limit files, e.g. `exclude: /node_modules/` so installed packages aren't converted again.

**Loader chains run right to left** (bottom to top in a list). For CSS:

- `css-loader` reads the CSS, follows its `@import` and `url()` references, and turns it into a JavaScript module.
- `style-loader` takes that result and adds it to the page inside a `<style>` tag.

So `use: ["style-loader", "css-loader"]` runs css-loader first.

Add `"sass-loader"` at the end of the list for **Sass**, an extended version of CSS with extras such as variables, which has to be converted to plain CSS. `"postcss-loader"`, placed between the other two, can add the browser-specific prefixes some CSS features still need.

Common loaders for code:

- `babel-loader` runs **Babel**, which rewrites newer JavaScript into older JavaScript that more browsers understand, and converts React's **JSX** (HTML-like tags written inside JavaScript). `swc-loader` and `esbuild-loader` do the same job much faster.
- `ts-loader` handles TypeScript. Alternatively, let Babel or SWC strip the types and run `tsc --noEmit` separately to check them.
- `css-loader` turns files named `*.module.css` into **CSS modules**: importing one gives you an object of class names made unique to that file.

Images and fonts don't need loaders in webpack 5; they use asset modules (a later lesson).
takeaways: `module.rules`: test + use (+ include/exclude)
Loader chains run right to left
style-loader + css-loader for CSS; babel, swc or esbuild loaders for JavaScript
Exclude node_modules from slow conversions
pitfalls: Writing `["css-loader", "style-loader"]`, which hands raw CSS to style-loader and fails.

quiz.explain: Loaders run right to left, so Sass is converted first, then css-loader runs, then style-loader.

concepts.name: Plugins: HTML, CSS extraction and defines
concepts.summary: Use HtmlWebpackPlugin to create index.html, MiniCssExtractPlugin to write CSS files, and DefinePlugin to paste values into your code at build time.
concepts.why: Real apps need an HTML page, CSS files and settings values, and plugins provide all three.
concepts.body:
A plugin is an object you add to the `plugins` list with `new`. Behind the scenes it has an `apply` method that webpack calls, so the plugin can step into the build. Built-in plugins live on the `webpack` object; others are npm packages you install.

**HtmlWebpackPlugin** (`html-webpack-plugin`) writes `index.html` for you, with `<script>` and `<link>` tags pointing at the bundles, content hashes and all. Give it `template: "./src/index.html"` to start from your own HTML file.

**MiniCssExtractPlugin** (`mini-css-extract-plugin`) writes CSS into separate `.css` files instead of adding it to the page from JavaScript, so the browser can download styles alongside the code. Use its `loader` in place of `style-loader`, usually only for production.

**DefinePlugin** (built in, `webpack.DefinePlugin`) finds names such as `__API_URL__` or `process.env.API_URL` in your code and replaces them while building. The value is pasted in **as code**, not as text, so wrap strings in `JSON.stringify`, which adds the quotes: `JSON.stringify("https://x")` gives `"https://x"`, quotes included.

Others you'll meet: **CopyWebpackPlugin** copies files your code doesn't import, such as `robots.txt`, and **BundleAnalyzerPlugin** (`webpack-bundle-analyzer`) draws a chart of what's inside your bundles.

`mode` already adds several plugins for you, such as minifying in production, so don't add those twice. And anything DefinePlugin pastes in ends up in the files every visitor downloads: never put secrets there.
takeaways: Plugins step into the build for everything loaders can't do
HtmlWebpackPlugin writes index.html with the right script tags
MiniCssExtractPlugin writes CSS files for production
DefinePlugin pastes in code: wrap strings in JSON.stringify
pitfalls: `new DefinePlugin({ API: 'https://x' })`, which pastes in an unquoted URL as code and breaks the bundle.

quiz.q: Why wrap DefinePlugin string values in JSON.stringify?
options: Values are pasted in as code, so strings need their quotes
quiz.explain: DefinePlugin replaces names with the code you give it; JSON.stringify turns text into a quoted string, which is valid code.

concepts.name: Asset modules: images, fonts and files
concepts.summary: Handle images, fonts and other files with webpack 5's built-in asset types instead of the old file-loader and url-loader.
concepts.why: Every app ships images and fonts, and webpack 5 handles them without extra loaders.
concepts.body: Every site ships images and fonts. Older webpack versions needed extra loaders for them (`file-loader`, `url-loader`, `raw-loader`). webpack 5 has **asset modules** built in instead: you pick one with a rule's `type`. - `asset/resource`: copy the file to the output folder; importing it gives you its URL. - `asset/inline`: importing gives you a **data URI**, a URL that starts with `data:` and holds the file itself, so no separate download is needed. - `asset/source`: importing gives you the file's contents as a string. - `asset`: choose by size. Files under 8 KB (about 8,000 bytes) become data URIs, bigger ones separate files. Change the limit with `parser.dataUrlCondition.maxSize`. Copied files are named by `output.assetModuleFilename` (default `[hash][ext][query]`) or by a rule's own `generator.filename`, such as `images/[name].[contenthash][ext]`. In JavaScript you can then write `import logoUrl from "./logo.png"` and put `logoUrl` in an ``. A `url(./bg.png)` inside CSS goes through the same rules, because css-loader turns it into an import. `new URL("./file.png", import.meta.url)` works too, and other bundlers understand it as well. Which to choose? A data URI saves one download, but it makes the bundle bigger, and the browser can't keep the image saved on its own between visits. Keep data URIs for tiny icons. To use SVG images as React components, add `@svgr/webpack`. When moving an old project to webpack 5, remove its file-loader rules, or each file gets processed twice.
takeaways: `asset/resource` = file + URL, `asset/inline` = data URI
`asset/source` = contents as a string, `asset` = chosen by size
Name files with `assetModuleFilename` or a rule's `generator.filename`
Drop file-loader and url-loader on webpack 5
pitfalls: Keeping old file-loader rules next to asset modules, so files are written twice.

quiz.q: Which asset type turns small files into data URIs and copies larger ones?

concepts.name: webpack-dev-server and HMR
concepts.summary: Run webpack-dev-server to rebuild as you save, update the open page with HMR, forward calls to your backend, and serve single-page apps.
concepts.why: A fast loop of save, look, fix depends on the dev server setup.
concepts.body:
Running `npx webpack` after every edit gets old fast. **webpack-dev-server** is a **dev server**: a small server program on your own computer that builds your app, serves it to your browser at an address like `http://localhost:8080`, and rebuilds whenever you save. Here localhost is your computer's name for itself, and 8080 is the **port**, the numbered door the server listens at. Start it with `npx webpack serve`.

It keeps the built files in memory instead of writing them to `dist/`, which is faster, so don't look for them there. It tells the open page about changes over a **WebSocket**: a connection that stays open so the server can send messages at any time.

**Hot module replacement (HMR)** is on by default (`hot: true`). When a module changes, webpack swaps the new version into the running page, as long as that module, or one that imports it, has said it can accept updates; such a module is an **HMR boundary**. Otherwise the page reloads. CSS added by style-loader updates instantly. For React, add `@pmmmwh/react-refresh-webpack-plugin` with `react-refresh`, so edited components update while keeping what's on screen.

Settings live under `devServer`:

- `port`, `host`, `open` (open a browser).
- `static`: folders served as they are, such as `public/`.
- `client.overlay`: show build errors on top of the page.

Many apps load one `index.html` and switch between screens with JavaScript, changing the address bar without asking the server for a new page: a **single-page application**. Reload on `/settings`, though, and the browser asks the server for `/settings`, which doesn't exist. `historyApiFallback: true` answers such unknown paths with `index.html`, and the app shows the right screen.

Your **backend**, the server program that holds data and answers your app's `fetch` calls, often runs separately, say on port 8000. Calling another port from the page runs into the browser's CORS rule. The `proxy` setting makes the dev server accept those calls and pass them on, acting as a **proxy**, so the browser only talks to one address. It takes a **list** of rules: `[{ context: ["/api"], target: "http://localhost:8000" }]`.

In plain modules, webpack's HMR controls are `module.hot` (CommonJS) or `import.meta.webpackHot` (ES modules), with `accept`, `dispose` and `invalidate`.

If you run your own Node server, for instance one that builds pages on the server, `webpack-dev-middleware` and `webpack-hot-middleware` add the same features to it. Like any dev server, never make it reachable from the internet: it isn't protected against attacks.
takeaways: `webpack serve` builds in memory and updates the page with HMR
`historyApiFallback` serves index.html for a single-page app's paths
`proxy` is a list of { context, target } rules
React needs react-refresh-webpack-plugin to keep what's on screen across edits
pitfalls: Looking for the dev server's output in dist/; it only exists in memory.

quiz.q: A single-page app shows 404 when you reload /settings in development. Which option fixes it?
quiz.explain: Unknown paths must fall back to index.html so the app's own JavaScript can show the right screen.

concepts.name: Module resolution and aliases
concepts.summary: Control how imports are found with resolve.extensions, alias, modules and conditionNames, and fallback for Node built-ins.
concepts.why: Import errors and duplicated packages usually come down to resolution settings.
concepts.body:
When webpack meets `import x from "something"`, its **resolver** decides which file that means: one in your project, or a package in node_modules. The `resolve` settings shape those decisions:

- `extensions`: endings to try when an import has none, e.g. `[".tsx", ".ts", ".js"]`. Keep the list short: each ending costs a look on disk for every import.
- `alias`: map a prefix to a folder. `"@": path.resolve(__dirname, "src")` makes `import "@/lib/api"` work from any folder. A trailing `$` means an exact match only (`react$`). Aliases can also force a single copy of a package, e.g. point `react` at one folder in a **monorepo** (one repository holding several of your own packages). For TypeScript, add the same mapping under `paths` in `tsconfig.json`.
- `modules`: folders searched for **bare imports**, imports by package name like `"react"`; the default is `["node_modules"]`.

`conditionNames` and `mainFields` choose which entries of a package's package.json webpack reads to find its files (`browser`, `module`, `import`, `require`...). Packages can point to different files for browsers and for Node; the defaults depend on the `target` setting.

**Node built-ins in the browser**: modules like `crypto` or `buffer` come with Node, not with browsers. webpack 4 quietly added browser versions of them, called **polyfills** (extra code that recreates a missing feature); webpack 5 doesn't. So either avoid them, add a polyfill yourself (`fallback: { buffer: require.resolve("buffer/") }`), or switch one off with `false`.

**"Fully specified" errors**: inside ES module packages (`.mjs` files, or `"type": "module"` in package.json), relative imports must include the file ending, as in browsers. `resolve.fullySpecified` controls this check.

To see why an import resolves the way it does, run `npx webpack --stats=detailed`, or temporarily set `infrastructureLogging: { level: "verbose" }`.
takeaways: `extensions`, `alias` and `modules` steer the resolver
webpack 5 doesn't polyfill Node built-ins: use `fallback`
Add the same aliases to tsconfig paths
Keep `extensions` short for speed
pitfalls: Expecting `require('crypto')` to work in browser code, as it did with webpack 4's automatic polyfills.

quiz.q: After upgrading to webpack 5, a dependency fails with "Can't resolve 'buffer'". Why?
options: webpack 5 stopped adding browser versions of Node's built-in modules
quiz.explain: You now have to add a polyfill with `resolve.fallback`, or replace the dependency.

concepts.name: Source maps and per-environment configs
concepts.summary: Pick a source map type for each mode, split settings into shared, dev and prod files with webpack-merge, and pass environment values.
concepts.why: Builds you can debug and settings you can maintain both depend on these choices.
concepts.body:
Bundled, minified code looks nothing like what you wrote, so an error at "line 1, position 48213" tells you little. A **source map** is a file that connects each part of the bundle back to your original files and lines. The browser's developer tools (the panel that opens with F12) and error-reporting services use it to show your real code.

The `devtool` option picks the kind of source map, trading build speed against accuracy:

- `eval-cheap-module-source-map` (or `eval-source-map`): fast rebuilds and good-enough mappings; typical for development.
- `source-map`: complete, separate `.map` files; best quality, slowest. Use it in production if you serve or upload maps.
- `hidden-source-map`: writes the maps but leaves out the `//# sourceMappingURL` comment that tells browsers where they are. Browsers won't download them, but you can upload them to an error-reporting service such as Sentry.
- `false`: no maps (the production default).

The words in those names mean: `eval` (each module wrapped in a call to JavaScript's `eval`, which makes rebuilds fast), `cheap` (line numbers only, not the exact spot in the line), `module` (map all the way back through loaders to your original files) and `inline` (the map is written inside the bundle as a data URL; never use it in production).

**Splitting the settings**: as your settings grow, keep shared settings in `webpack.common.js` and combine them with a development or production file using the `webpack-merge` package. Or export a function and branch on `argv.mode`. Pick one approach and stick to it.

**Environment values**: `webpack.config.js` runs in Node, so it can read `process.env`. Pass only what the browser code needs, through DefinePlugin or `EnvironmentPlugin`; the `dotenv-webpack` plugin loads `.env` files. Again: everything you pass ends up in the files every visitor downloads.
takeaways: Development: eval-cheap-module-source-map; production: source-map or hidden-source-map
`inline` maps never belong in production
webpack-merge combines shared and mode-specific settings
Pass only what browser code needs through EnvironmentPlugin or DefinePlugin
pitfalls: Shipping `eval` or `inline` source maps in production bundles.

quiz.q: Which devtool creates maps that browsers won't load but an error-reporting service can use?
quiz.explain: hidden-source-map leaves out the sourceMappingURL comment, so nothing on the public site points to the maps.

concepts.name: Code splitting and SplitChunksPlugin
concepts.summary: Split bundles with dynamic import(), magic comments and prefetching, and tune SplitChunksPlugin's cache groups for package code.
concepts.why: Sending less JavaScript up front is the biggest lever for how fast a page loads.
concepts.body:
**Code splitting** means cutting your app into several chunks, so the browser downloads only what the current page needs and fetches the rest later. webpack makes separate chunks in three ways:

- **Entry points**: each entry gets its own chunk. Code that two entries share is copied into both, unless you set up sharing.
- **Dynamic imports**: `import("./chart.js")` returns a promise, and webpack puts that module and its imports in a chunk downloaded only when the line runs. Splitting a React app per page with `React.lazy` uses this.
- **SplitChunksPlugin** (`optimization.splitChunks`): moves shared modules and package code into common chunks.

**Magic comments** are special comments inside `import()` that webpack reads. `import(/* webpackChunkName: "chart" */ "./chart.js")` names the chunk; `webpackPrefetch: true` downloads it when the browser is idle, ready for later; `webpackPreload: true` downloads it at the same time as the chunk that imports it.

By default SplitChunksPlugin only splits chunks loaded on demand. Set `chunks: "all"` to split the starting chunks too, so package code shared by several entries is downloaded once. **Cache groups** decide how modules are grouped:

- `defaultVendors` collects modules from `node_modules`; `default` collects modules used by at least two chunks.
- Add your own, e.g. a `react` group for React's packages with a higher `priority`.
- `minSize` (20 KB by default; smaller groups aren't split out), `maxSize`, `minChunks`, `maxAsyncRequests` and `maxInitialRequests` limit how far splitting goes.

Check the result with `webpack-bundle-analyzer`. Too many tiny chunks mean many small requests, each with its own fixed cost. One giant package chunk has the opposite problem: updating any single package changes its content hash, so every visitor downloads the whole thing again.
takeaways: Dynamic import() creates chunks downloaded on demand
Magic comments: webpackChunkName, webpackPrefetch, webpackPreload
`splitChunks.chunks: 'all'` shares package code across entries
Cache groups with priorities control grouping
pitfalls: Prefetching everything, which wastes users' data on chunks they rarely need.

quiz.q: By default, which chunks does SplitChunksPlugin split?
options: Only chunks loaded on demand (dynamic imports)
quiz.explain: The default is `chunks: 'async'`; set 'all' to include the starting chunks.

concepts.name: Long-term caching and persistent cache
concepts.summary: Keep content hashes stable across builds with a separate runtime chunk and stable ids, and speed up rebuilds with the filesystem cache.
concepts.why: Users should only download again what changed, and developers shouldn't wait for work that didn't change.
concepts.body:
Two different kinds of caching matter with webpack: browsers keeping your output files between visits, and webpack keeping its own work between builds.

**Browsers keeping files.** With `[contenthash]` in file names, unchanged files keep their names and stay saved in visitors' browsers. To keep those hashes truly stable:

- `optimization.runtimeChunk: "single"` moves the webpack runtime into its own file. The runtime contains a list of every chunk's file name. Without this, adding a chunk loaded on demand changes that list inside your main bundle, and with it the main bundle's hash.
- `optimization.moduleIds: "deterministic"` and `chunkIds: "deterministic"` (production defaults in webpack 5) give modules and chunks numbers that stay the same when unrelated modules are added.
- Put rarely changing package code in its own chunk.
- Serve hashed files with `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable` (keep for a year), and `index.html` with no caching.

**webpack keeping its work.** `cache: { type: "filesystem" }` saves webpack's results to `node_modules/.cache/webpack`, so the second and later builds are dramatically faster. That works in CI too, if you keep that folder between runs.

Tell webpack what should throw the saved results away: `cache.buildDependencies: { config: [__filename] }` means "start fresh when this settings file changes", and `cache.version` lets you force a fresh start by hand. In development mode the default is a cache in memory, lost when webpack stops.

If builds behave strangely after upgrading packages, delete the cache folder first.
takeaways: contenthash + a separate runtime chunk + `deterministic` ids = stable hashes
Package chunks change rarely and stay saved in browsers
`cache: { type: 'filesystem' }` speeds up rebuilds and CI
Declare buildDependencies so a config change starts a fresh cache
pitfalls: Leaving the runtime inside the main chunk, so every new page loaded on demand changes the main bundle's hash.

quiz.q: Why move the runtime out with `runtimeChunk: 'single'`?
options: Its list of chunk file names changes often and would change other bundles' hashes
quiz.explain: Keeping that list in its own small file keeps the main and package hashes stable.

concepts.name: Tree shaking and sideEffects
concepts.summary: Get unused code removed with ES modules, usedExports, the sideEffects flag and scope hoisting, and know what breaks it.
concepts.why: Unused package code is often the largest part of a bundle.
concepts.body:
**Tree shaking** leaves out exports that nothing imports, like shaking a tree so the dead leaves fall. In webpack it takes several steps working together, all on in production mode:

- `optimization.usedExports`: webpack marks which exports of each module are actually used.
- The minifier, **Terser**, then deletes the unused code, which nothing refers to anymore.
- `optimization.sideEffects`: if a package says `"sideEffects": false` in its package.json, meaning "importing my files does nothing by itself", webpack can skip **whole modules** whose exports aren't used, even ones pulled in through an index file that re-exports everything.
- `optimization.concatenateModules` (**scope hoisting**): webpack joins modules into one shared scope instead of wrapping each in its own function, so the output is smaller and faster.

What breaks it:

- **CommonJS** (`require`, `module.exports`): webpack 5 understands some uses, but ES modules are far more reliable. Make sure Babel doesn't turn your `import`s into `require`s (`modules: false` in preset-env; babel-loader already keeps ES modules by default).
- **Code that does something just by being imported**: polyfills, global CSS imports, registering things at the top of a module. If you mark a package `"sideEffects": false`, list the files that do have side effects, `"sideEffects": ["*.css", "./src/polyfills.js"]`, or your CSS disappears.
- Importing everything as one object (`import * as lib`) and picking from it by a computed name (`lib[name]`): webpack can't tell which parts you use.

Mark a function call with `/*#__PURE__*/` to promise the minifier that the call has no side effects, so it may drop the call when the result is unused. To check what happened, use the bundle analyzer, or build with `mode: "development"` plus `usedExports` and look for `/* unused harmony export */` comments.
takeaways: Tree shaking needs ES modules
usedExports marks unused code; the minifier removes it
`sideEffects: false` lets webpack skip whole modules
List CSS and polyfills in sideEffects so they survive
pitfalls: Setting `"sideEffects": false` in an app that imports global CSS, silently dropping the styles.

quiz.q: Why can `"sideEffects": false` make global CSS imports disappear?
options: It only affects production source maps
webpack may drop imports whose exports go unused, and a CSS import's exports are never used
quiz.explain: CSS imports exist only for their side effect, so they must be listed in sideEffects.

concepts.name: Module Federation and micro-frontends
concepts.summary: Load code from separately deployed builds while the page runs, with Module Federation's remotes, exposes and shared single copies.
concepts.why: Large organizations use it to assemble one website from parts that different teams deploy on their own.
concepts.body:
Picture a shop site where one team owns checkout and another owns search, and each wants to deploy without waiting for the other. **Module Federation** (webpack 5's `ModuleFederationPlugin`) lets one build load modules from another build **while the page is running**, not at build time. Sites assembled this way are often called **micro-frontends**: one frontend made of separately deployed parts.

Each build plays one or both roles:

- A **remote app** `exposes` modules (`"./Cart": "./src/Cart.jsx"`) and writes a small `remoteEntry.js` file listing them.
- A **host app** declares `remotes` (`checkout: "checkout@https://cdn.example.com/checkout/remoteEntry.js"`) and imports from them like packages: `import("checkout/Cart")`.

**Shared dependencies** are agreed on while the page loads. With `shared: { react: { singleton: true, requiredVersion: "^19.0.0" } }`, the host app and its remotes use a single copy of React instead of each bringing their own; React breaks when two copies run together. If versions don't match, you get a warning or separate copies, depending on the settings.

Practical rules:

- The host app must load shared modules asynchronously, so use a **bootstrap** entry: `index.js` contains only `import("./bootstrap")`, which gives the runtime a moment to agree on shared versions first. Skip it and you get "Shared module is not available for eager consumption", meaning it was needed immediately at startup.
- Treat exposed modules as promises to other teams: version them and change them carefully. Separate deploys mean one team's mistake can break another team's page while it runs, so wrap remote loads in React error boundaries (components that catch errors and show a fallback).
- Sharing TypeScript types, choosing remotes while running and runtime plugins come from **Module Federation 2.0** (`@module-federation/enhanced`), which also works with Rspack, Vite and other bundlers.

Federation solves an organizational problem, many teams deploying one large frontend independently, at the price of complexity in the running page. A monorepo with shared packages is often simpler.
takeaways: Remote apps expose modules via remoteEntry.js; host apps import them while running
`singleton: true` keeps one copy of React across all builds
Use an async bootstrap entry for shared modules
Federation trades complexity in the page for independent deploys
pitfalls: Importing shared modules directly in the host's entry file, causing 'not available for eager consumption'.

quiz.q: What does `singleton: true` on a shared dependency ensure?
options: The dependency is bundled into every remote
Only one copy is loaded and used across host and remotes
It is downloaded from npm while running
quiz.explain: A single copy is essential for libraries like React, which break when several copies run.

concepts.name: Writing loaders and plugins
concepts.summary: Write a loader as a function that rewrites a file's code, and a plugin that attaches to webpack's compiler and compilation hooks through Tapable.
concepts.why: Custom build steps in large codebases are written as loaders and plugins.
concepts.body:
A loader is just a function, exported from a module, that receives a file's contents as a string and returns new contents. Inside it, `this` is the loader context, with helpers:

- `this.getOptions()` reads the rule's `options`; you can pass it a schema (a description of the allowed options) to check them.
- `this.resourcePath` is the file being processed; `this.addDependency(file)` tells webpack to rebuild when another file changes too.
- Return a string, or call `this.callback(err, content, sourceMap)` to pass a source map along. For asynchronous work, call `const done = this.async()` and later `done(...)`.

Loaders should give the same output for the same input, so webpack can reuse results: they're cached by default, and `this.cacheable(false)` opts out. A loader can also have a `pitch` method, which runs before the chain, left to right, and can cut the chain short.

A plugin is a class with `apply(compiler)`. webpack's internals are built on **Tapable**, a small library of **hooks**: named moments in the build that plugins can attach functions to (webpack calls this "tapping").

- The **compiler** object, passed to `apply`, runs the whole process. Its hooks include `beforeRun`, `compile`, `thisCompilation`, `emit`, `done` and `watchRun`.
- A **compilation** is one build of the dependency graph; watch mode makes a new one for every rebuild. In `thisCompilation`, tap `compilation.hooks.processAssets` with a `stage` (e.g. `PROCESS_ASSETS_STAGE_ADDITIONAL`) to add or change output files with `compilation.emitAsset` and `webpack.sources`.
- Hooks can be synchronous (`tap`), callback-based (`tapAsync`) or promise-based (`tapPromise`).

To report problems, push a `new webpack.WebpackError(...)` onto `compilation.errors` in a plugin, or call `this.emitError` in a loader, instead of throwing a bare exception that stops the build with a confusing message.
takeaways: Loaders: functions from code to code, with this.getOptions, callback and async
Plugins: `apply(compiler)` attaching to Tapable hooks
Change output in `processAssets` at the right stage
Report errors through webpack instead of throwing
pitfalls: Changing output files in the old `emit` hook, which is deprecated (still works but due to be removed), instead of a `processAssets` stage.

quiz.q: Which hook should a plugin use to add a new output file in webpack 5?
quiz.explain: processAssets, with a suitable stage, is the supported place to add or change output files.

concepts.name: Internals and build performance
concepts.summary: Understand the module graph, chunk graph and runtime, measure slow builds, and know when to switch to faster loaders or Rspack.
concepts.why: Large webpack builds can take minutes; understanding the internals points to the real fixes.
concepts.body:
Inside one build, webpack first makes a **module graph**: every module and which one imports which. From it, it makes a **chunk graph**: which modules go into which chunks, and which chunks load which others.

The webpack runtime in the output brings this to life with a function called `__webpack_require__`. It keeps a table of modules (each module's code wrapped in a function), a cache of modules that have already run, and code that downloads chunks, either by adding `<script>` tags or with `import()` for ES module output. Build with `mode: "development"` and `devtool: false`, then read the bundle, and you can see all of this.

Where the time goes in slow builds, usually:

- **Loaders**, especially Babel, and `ts-loader` when it also checks types. Switch to `swc-loader` or `esbuild-loader`, and check types in a separate process (`fork-ts-checker-webpack-plugin` or `tsc --noEmit`).
- **Minifying**: use the SWC or esbuild minifier through `TerserPlugin.swcMinify` or `TerserPlugin.esbuildMinify`.
- **Source maps**: the high-quality kinds are expensive in development.
- **Needless work**: rules without `include`/`exclude`, long `resolve.extensions` lists, building translations nobody uses (moment.js locales), and no filesystem cache.

Measure before changing anything: `npx webpack --profile --json > stats.json` for the bundle analyzer, `speed-measure-webpack-plugin` for time per loader, and `ProgressPlugin` for time per phase.

When a codebase outgrows these fixes, Rspack (written in Rust, accepting webpack's settings and most loaders and plugins) often builds 5 to 10 times faster with modest migration effort, while new projects usually choose Vite.
takeaways: Module graph -> chunk graph -> runtime with __webpack_require__
Loaders, minifiers and source maps take most of the build time
Measure with --profile --json and per-loader timings
Rspack is the nearly drop-in path to much faster builds
pitfalls: Changing settings blindly without measuring which loader or plugin is slow.

quiz.q: What does `__webpack_require__` do with a module that has already run?
quiz.explain: The runtime keeps a cache of modules, so each module's code runs only once.
